tier_reason: The README carries a first-party '~50 times faster than an ordinary Smith-Waterman' sentence with no comparison program, data, compiler, flags or CPU model, and its E. coli CPU-time figures (AMD ~880 s / ~460 s, Intel ~960 s / ~500 s, ~40 MB) have no baseline column. The PLoS ONE 2013 paper is peer-reviewed but could not be opened (doi.org, journals.plos.org, PMC and ar5iv all blocked or unresolvable); search snippets say it compares SSW with SSEARCH 36.3.5c and Farrar's striped SW, not with an ordinary scalar SW, so it cannot lift the tier from here.

corrections.caveats: The '~50 times' headline names no comparison program, data, compiler, flags or hardware, and the README's E. coli CPU-time figures have no baseline column. The PLoS ONE 2013 paper (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0082138; arXiv 1208.6350) could not be opened here (doi.org, journals.plos.org, PMC and arXiv blocked); per search snippets only, it benchmarks SSW single-threaded on a 2 GHz x86-64 AMD machine against Farrar's striped SW and SSEARCH 36.3.5c and finds SSW fastest or equally fast on protein database search, with no quoted multiple and no ordinary (non-SIMD) SW baseline seen. The abstract says MOSAIK, SCISSORS, TANGRAM and RZMBLR got faster after swapping their ordinary or banded SW module for SSW. It is a SIMD application library (sequence alignment) rather than a general SIMD intrinsics library. The LICENSE.txt (MIT) file was only added on 2026-01-15; earlier releases carried the licence in source headers.

notes: README numbers match the record; metadata checked on github.com (MIT LICENSE.txt, 323 stars, 119 forks, last commit 2026-01-15 'added LICENSE.txt file', not archived or a fork). Kept at C: the 50x claim is first-party with no methodology and the paper's own comparison is against SIMD incumbents (SSEARCH, Farrar), not the record's ordinary-SW baseline; a paper-access retier could move it to B against SSEARCH if Figure 2 is read. Category fit is loose (bioinformatics alignment library using SSE2/NEON via sse2neon).

tier_reason: The README table (Ryzen 1600, rdtsc cycles per byte) compares the SSSE3 fast path against the library's own scalar slow path (-b=0) using the public FileConverter demo (src/tests/FileConverter.cpp); the compiler for the table is only implied by the FileConverter_msvc.exe sample commands, with no MSVC version, and the baseline is the project's own fallback rather than an incumbent, so it stays first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the table. The sample benchmark commands run FileConverter_msvc.exe, which scripts/build_msvc_file_conv.cmd builds with cl /O2 /Oi /EHsc /MD /D NDEBUG /D TIMING (MSVC version not given); non-MSVC builds need -mssse3 -std=c++11.
corrections.caveats: The comparison is against the library's own scalar slow path (-b=0, which forces validate mode), not against iconv, ICU or another incumbent; the fast-path row uses -m=2, which is cmValidate, so both rows validate. Each run converts one ~1 MB array from RAM to RAM repeatedly, so the large lookup table stays warm; the README warns it barely fits in cache and that performance depends on the code-point length mix. The compiler for the table is only implied (MSVC build of FileConverter, version unstated). The README's blog article with broader comparisons is on dirtyhandscoding.github.io, which is blocked here. Per search snippets only, Lemire and Mula's peer-reviewed 'Transcoding Billions of Unicode Characters per Second with SIMD Instructions' (Software: Practice and Experience 52(2), 2022; arXiv 2109.10433, blocked here) benchmarks utf8lut beside ICU, LLVM, u8u16 and utf8sse4 and reports that u8u16 and utf8sse4 often beat it on European-language text because utf8lut has no ASCII fast path; utf8lut-versus-ICU numbers were not seen. README calls it mainly a proof of concept. Repo migrated from Bitbucket and last changed in 2020.

notes: All four cycles-per-byte pairs match the README and the derived ratios (9.3x, 13x, 9.1x, 7.2x) are correct. Metadata checked on github.com: BSL-1.0, 11 stars, 2 forks, last commit 2020-04-19 (abandoned). It is a UTF-8/UTF-16 transcoder, so a category override to wave 3's unicode-utf8 (with the matching domain override) would fit better than simd-intrinsics-libraries; the Lemire-Mula SPE paper could support a retier against ICU if it can be opened.

tier_reason: benchmarks/pixel-by-pixel.md's WebAssembly table compares @blazediff/core-wasm with pixelmatch in the same tinybench run (apps/image-benchmark/src/pixel-by-pixel/blazediff-core-wasm-benchmark.ts, both called without an output buffer at default threshold 0.1), the build flags are public (crates/blazediff/scripts/build-wasm.sh RUSTFLAGS +simd128,+bulk-memory, crates/Cargo.toml release profile opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1), and BENCHMARKS.md names the Apple M1 Max and Node.js 22.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust (rustc version not stated), cargo build --release for wasm32-unknown-unknown with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+simd128,+bulk-memory' and the workspace release profile in crates/Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, lto = "fat", codegen-units 1, panic = abort), wasm-bindgen 0.2.100 post-processing, then wasm-opt -O3 only if wasm-opt is installed (crates/blazediff/scripts/build-wasm.sh); harness apps/image-benchmark (tinybench 5, pixelmatch ^7.2.0) under Node.js 22.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark, measured in Node.js 22 on an Apple M1 Max, not in a browser. In the wasm run pixelmatch is 1.5-1.9x slower on the large differing fixtures than in the same page's JS run (4k/1 332.26 ms vs 201.60 ms, 4k/3 423.14 vs 253.77, page/2 513.06 vs 267.84) while small and identical rows agree, so the headline 4k/1 ratio of about 10x is about 6.1x against the JS-run pixelmatch time (derived from page data). Whether wasm-opt ran on the measured module is not recorded, and the rustc version is not stated. Results differ slightly from pixelmatch (counts within ~0.05%, e.g. 4k/1 69,932 vs 69,912 pixels). Byte-identical pairs used to be a 60-70% loss; pixel-by-pixel.md says skipping a scalar memcmp shortcut on wasm32 turned them into small wins (4k/2 identical 22.70 ms vs 22.17 ms). On identical pairs the plain JS @blazediff/core (2.50 ms for 4k/1) is far faster than the wasm build (17.47 ms).

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the wasm table of benchmarks/pixel-by-pixel.md (~50.8% average, 4k/1 332.26 vs 33.18 ms, 4k/3 423.14 vs 44.65, blazediff/1 1.24 vs 0.24, 4k/2 identical 22.70 vs 22.17); the harness is a fair same-process comparison with matching options. Main shortcoming: pixelmatch ran markedly slower in the wasm run than in the JS run on large differing images, inflating the 10x headline (about 6x against the JS-run figure). Metadata checked: MIT, 351 stars, 5 forks, last commit 2026-09-21; the aslang-registry copy is already a recorded duplicate.
